danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: I november 1805 måtte fyrst Vasilij ud på en inspektionsrejse i fire forskellige provinser. Han havde arrangeret dette for sig selv, så han samtidig kunne besøge sine forsømte godser, og undervejs hente sin søn Anatole, hvor hans regiment lå, for at tage ham med på besøg hos fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij og arrangere et parti for ham med den rige gamle mands datter. Men inden han forlod hjemmet og kastede sig over disse nye affærer, måtte fyrst Vasilij ordne sagerne med Pierre, som ganske vist i den seneste tid havde tilbragt hele dage hjemme — det vil sige i fyrst Vasilijs hus, hvor han boede — og havde været absurd, ophidset og fjollet i Hélènes nærhed (som en forelsket bør være), men endnu ikke havde friet til hende.

»Alt det her er meget fint, men tingene må bringes i orden,« sagde fyrst Vasilij til sig selv med et bedrøvet suk en morgen, da han følte, at Pierre, som stod i en sådan gæld til ham (»men lad det ligge«), ikke opførte sig helt rigtigt i denne sag. »Ungdom, letsindighed... nå, Gud være med ham,« tænkte han og nød sin egen hjertensgodhed, »men det må bringes til en afgørelse. I overmorgen er det Ljoljas navnedag. Jeg inviterer to-tre mennesker, og hvis han ikke forstår, hvad han bør gøre, så bliver det min sag — ja, min sag. Jeg er hendes far.«

Seks uger efter Anna Pavlovnas »at home« og efter den søvnløse nat, hvor han havde besluttet, at det ville være en ulykke at gifte sig med Hélène, og at han burde undgå hende og rejse bort, var Pierre trods den beslutning stadig ikke rejst fra fyrst Vasilijs hus og følte med rædsel, at han i folks øjne dag for dag blev mere og mere knyttet til hende, at det var umuligt for ham at vende tilbage til sin tidligere opfattelse af hende, at han ikke kunne løsrive sig fra hende, og at det, skønt det ville være forfærdeligt, ville blive nødvendigt at forene sin skæbne med hendes. Han kunne måske have frigjort sig, men fyrst Vasilij, der sjældent før havde holdt selskab, lod nu næppe en dag gå uden et aftenselskab, hvor Pierre måtte være til stede, medmindre han ønskede at ødelægge den almindelige glæde og skuffe alles forventninger. Fyrst Vasilij ville i de sjældne øjeblikke, hvor han var hjemme, tage Pierres hånd i forbifarten og trække den nedad, eller fraværende byde sin rynkede, glatbarberede kind frem til Pierres kys og sige: »Til i morgen,« eller: »Bliv hjemme til middag, ellers ser jeg dig ikke,« eller: »Jeg bliver hjemme for din skyld,« og lignende. Og skønt fyrst Vasilij, når han blev hjemme (som han sagde) for Pierres skyld, næppe vekslede to ord med ham, følte Pierre sig ude af stand til at skuffe ham. Hver dag sagde han det samme til sig selv: »Det er på tide, jeg forstår hende og gør mig klart, hvad hun virkelig er. Tog jeg fejl før, eller tager jeg fejl nu? Nej, hun er ikke dum, hun er en fortræffelig pige,« sagde han undertiden til sig selv. »Hun begår aldrig en fejl, siger aldrig noget dumt. Hun siger lidt, men det, hun siger, er altid klart og ligetil, så hun er ikke dum. Hun var aldrig forlegen og er det heller ikke nu, så hun kan ikke være en dårlig kvinde!« Han havde ofte begyndt at anstille betragtninger eller tænke højt i hendes selskab, og hun havde altid svaret ham enten med en kort, men passende bemærkning — der viste, at det ikke interesserede hende — eller med et tavst blik og et smil, der mere håndgribeligt end alt andet viste Pierre hendes overlegenhed. Hun havde ret i at betragte alle argumenter som vrøvl i sammenligning med det smil.

Hun henvendte sig altid til ham med et strålende, tillidsfuldt smil, kun beregnet for ham, hvori der var noget mere betydningsfuldt end i det almindelige smil, der normalt oplyste hendes ansigt. Pierre vidste, at alle ventede på, at han skulle sige ét ord og krydse en bestemt grænse, og han vidste, at han før eller siden ville tage skridtet, men en ubegribelig rædsel greb ham ved tanken om det forfærdelige skridt. Tusind gange i den halvanden måned, hvor han følte sig draget nærmere og nærmere den frygtelige afgrund, sagde Pierre til sig selv: »Hvad gør jeg? Jeg har brug for beslutsomhed. Kan det være, at jeg ingen har?«

Han ønskede at tage en beslutning, men følte med forfærdelse, at han i denne sag manglede den viljestyrke, han havde kendt hos sig selv og virkelig besad. Pierre var en af dem, der kun er stærke, når de føler sig helt uskyldige, og siden den dag, han var blevet overvældet af en følelse af begær, da han bøjede sig over snustobaksdåsen hos Anna Pavlovna, havde en ubevidst skyldfølelse over dette begær lammet hans vilje.

På Hélènes navnedag var et lille selskab af nære venner — som hans hustru sagde — samlet til aftensmad hos fyrst Vasilij. Alle disse venner og slægtninge havde fået at forstå, at den unge piges skæbne ville blive afgjort den aften. Gæsterne sad til bords. Fyrstinde Kuragina, en svær, imponerende kvinde, der engang havde været smuk, sad for bordenden. Til begge sider af hende sad de fornemste gæster — en gammel general og hans hustru og Anna Pavlovna Scherer. I den anden ende sad de yngre og mindre vigtige gæster, og dér sad også familiens medlemmer og Pierre og Hélène side om side. Fyrst Vasilij spiste ikke; han gik rundt om bordet i godt humør og satte sig snart hos én, snart hos en anden af gæsterne. Til hver af dem kom han med en ligegyldig og elskværdig bemærkning — undtagen til Pierre og Hélène, hvis tilstedeværelse han syntes ikke at bemærke. Han livede hele selskabet op. Vokslysene brændte klart, sølvet og krystallet glimtede, ligesom damernes toiletter og mændenes guld- og sølvepauletter; tjenere i skarlagenrøde livréer bevægede sig rundt om bordet, og klapren af tallerkener, knive og glas blandede sig med den livlige summen af adskillige samtaler. Ved den ene bordende hørtes den gamle kammerherre forsikre en gammel baronesse, at han elskede hende lidenskabeligt, hvilket hun lo af; ved den anden ende hørtes historien om en vis Marja Viktorovnas ulykker. I midten af bordet tiltrak fyrst Vasilij sig alles opmærksomhed. Med et skælmsk smil fortalte han damerne om onsdagens møde i Rigsrådet, hvor Sergej Kuzmitj Vjazmitinovs, den nye militærguvernør i Petersborg, havde modtaget og oplæst kejser Alexanders da berømte reskript fra hæren til Sergej Kuzmitj, hvori kejseren sagde, at han fra alle sider modtog forsikringer om folkets troskab, at erklæringen fra Petersborg glædede ham særligt, og at han var stolt over at stå i spidsen for en sådan nation og ville stræbe efter at være den værdig. Reskriptet begyndte med ordene: »Sergej Kuzmitj, Fra alle sider når mig beretninger,« og så videre.
»Nå, og så kom han ikke længere end til 'Sergej Kuzmitj'?« spurgte en af damerne.

»Præcis, ikke et hår længere,« svarede fyrst Vasilij leende. »'Sergej Kuzmitj... Fra alle sider... Fra alle sider... Sergej Kuzmitj...' Stakkels Vjazmitinovs kunne ikke komme videre! Han begyndte reskriptet om og om igen, men så snart han sagde 'Sergej,' hulkede han — 'Kuz-mitj' — tårer — og 'Fra alle sider' druknede i hulk, og han kunne ikke komme videre. Og atter lommetørklædet, og atter: 'Sergej Kuzmitj, Fra alle sider...' og tårer, til man endelig bad en anden om at læse det.«
»Kuzmitj... Fra alle sider... og så tårer,« gentog nogen leende.
»Vær nu ikke uvenlig,« udbrød Anna Pavlovna fra sin bordende og løftede en truende finger. »Han er en så værdig og fortræffelig mand, vores kære Vjazmitinovs...«

Alle lo hjerteligt. For bordenden, hvor de fornemste gæster sad, syntes alle at være i strålende humør og under indflydelse af en mangfoldighed af muntre stemninger. Kun Pierre og Hélène sad tavse side om side, næsten for bordenden, med et undertrykt smil, der oplyste begges ansigter, et smil der intet havde med Sergej Kuzmitj at gøre — et smil af undseelse over deres egne følelser. Men hvor meget alle de andre end lo, talte og spøgte, hvor meget de end nød deres Rhinskvin, sauté og is, og hvor meget de end undgik at se på det unge par, og hvor ligeglade og uopmærksomme de end forekom — kunne man af de lejlighedsvise blikke, de kastede, fornemme, at historien om Sergej Kuzmitj, latteren og maden alt sammen var et påskud, og at hele selskabets opmærksomhed i virkeligheden var rettet mod — Pierre og Hélène. Fyrst Vasilij efterlignede Sergej Kuzmitjs hulken, og samtidig gled hans blik over til datteren, og mens han lo, sagde hans ansigtsudtryk tydeligt: »Ja... det nærmer sig, det hele afgøres i dag.« Anna Pavlovna truede ham på vegne af »vores kære Vjazmitinovs,« og i hendes øjne, der et øjeblik gled til Pierre, læste fyrst Vasilij en lykønskning med hans kommende svigersøn og med datterens lykke. Den gamle fyrstinde sukkede bedrøvet, da hun bød den gamle dame ved sin side vin, og hendes suk syntes at sige: »Ja, for dig og mig er der intet andet end at nippe til sød vin, min kære — nu da tiden er kommet for disse unge til at være så dristigt, udfordrende lykkelige.« »Og hvilket vrøvl alt det her er, som jeg siger!« tænkte en diplomat og sendte et blik mod de lykkeliges ansigter. »Det dér er lykke!«

Ind i de ubetydelige, trivielle og kunstige interesser, der forenede dette selskab, var trådt den simple følelse af tiltrækning mellem en sund og smuk ung mand og kvinde. Og denne menneskelige følelse dominerede alt andet og svævede over al deres affekterede snak. Vittigheder faldt til jorden, nyheder var ikke interessante, og livligheden var tydeligvis tvungen. Ikke blot gæsterne, men selv tjenerne, der ventede ved bordet, syntes at mærke det og glemte deres pligter, mens de kiggede på den smukke Hélène med hendes strålende ansigt og på Pierres røde, brede og lykkelige, omend urolige ansigt. Det var, som om selve lysenes skær var samlet om de to lykkelige ansigter alene.

Pierre følte, at han var midtpunkt for det hele, og dette både glædede og forlegede ham. Han var som en mand, der er helt opslugt af en gerning. Han hverken så, hørte eller forstod noget tydeligt. Kun nu og da trængte løsrevne tanker og indtryk fra den virkelige verden uventet ind i hans sind.

»Så det er altså afgjort!« tænkte han. »Og hvordan er det sket? Hvor hurtigt! Nu ved jeg, at det ikke er for hendes skyld alene, eller for min egen, men for alles skyld, at det uundgåeligt må ske. De forventer det alle, de er så sikre på, at det vil ske, at jeg ikke kan, jeg kan ikke skuffe dem. Men hvordan bliver det? Det ved jeg ikke, men det sker med sikkerhed!« tænkte Pierre og sendte et blik mod de blændende skuldre, der var så tæt på hans øjne.

Eller han følte sig pludselig flov, han vidste ikke over hvad. Han syntes, det var pinligt at tiltrække alles opmærksomhed og at blive betragtet som en heldig mand, der med sit jævne ansigt blev set som en slags Paris i besiddelse af en Helena. »Men tvivl ikke — det er altid og må altid være sådan!« trøstede han sig. »Og desuden, hvad har jeg gjort for at fremkalde det? Hvordan begyndte det? Jeg rejste fra Moskva med fyrst Vasilij. Dengang var der intet. Så hvorfor skulle jeg ikke bo i hans hus? Så spillede jeg kort med hende og samlede hendes reticule op og kørte ud med hende. Hvordan begyndte det, hvornår skete det?« Og der sad han nu ved hendes side som hendes forlovede, mens han så, hørte og mærkede hendes nærhed, hendes åndedræt, hendes bevægelser, hendes skønhed. Og så forekom det ham pludselig, at det ikke var hende, men ham der var så usædvanligt smuk, og at det var derfor, alle kiggede på ham, og smigret af denne almindelige beundring rettede han brystet, løftede hovedet og frydede sig over sin lykke. Pludselig hørte han en velkendt stemme, der gentog noget til ham for anden gang. Men Pierre var så fordybet, at han ikke forstod, hvad der blev sagt.
»Jeg spørger, hvornår De sidst hørte fra Bolkonskij,« gentog fyrst Vasilij for tredje gang. »Hvor fraværende De dog er, min kære.«

Fyrst Vasilij smilede, og Pierre bemærkede, at alle smilede af ham og Hélène. »Nå, hvad gør det, når I alle ved det?« tænkte Pierre. »Hvad så? Det er sandheden!« og han smilede selv sit milde, barnlige smil, og Hélène smilede også.
»Hvornår fik De brevet? Var det fra Olmütz?« gentog fyrst Vasilij, der lod, som om han ønskede at vide det for at afgøre en uoverensstemmelse.
»Hvordan kan man tale eller tænke på sådanne bagateller?« tænkte Pierre.
»Ja, fra Olmütz,« svarede han med et suk.

Efter aftensmaden fulgte Pierre med sin ledsagerinde de andre ind i salonen. Gæsterne begyndte at bryde op — nogle uden at tage afsked med Hélène. Andre, som om de ikke ville forstyrre hende i en vigtig beskæftigelse, kom hen til hende et øjeblik og skyndte sig bort, idet de nægtede at lade hende følge dem til dørs. Diplomaten bevarede en sorgmodig tavshed, da han forlod salonen. Han forestillede sig den forfængelighed, hans diplomatiske karriere repræsenterede sammenlignet med Pierres lykke. Den gamle general brummede til sin hustru, da hun spurgte til hans ben. »Åh, det gamle fjols,« tænkte han. »Den der prinsesse Hélène vil stadig være smuk, når hun er halvtreds.«
»Jeg tror, jeg tør lykønske Dem,« hviskede Anna Pavlovna til den gamle fyrstinde og kyssede hende hjerteligt. »Hvis blot jeg ikke havde denne hovedpine, ville jeg være blevet længere.«
Den gamle fyrstinde svarede ikke; hun var pint af jalousi over datterens lykke.

Mens gæsterne tog afsked, forblev Pierre i lang tid alene med Hélène i den lille salon, hvor de sad. Han havde ofte før i de seneste seks uger været alene med hende, men havde aldrig talt til hende om kærlighed. Nu følte han, at det var uundgåeligt, men han kunne ikke beslutte sig til at tage det afgørende skridt. Han skammede sig; han følte, at han optog en andens plads her ved siden af Hélène. »Denne lykke er ikke for dig,« hviskede en indre stemme ham i øret. »Denne lykke er for dem, der ikke har i sig, hvad du har.«

Men da han nu var nødt til at sige noget, begyndte han med at spørge, om hun var tilfreds med festen. Hun svarede på sin sædvanligt ligefremme måde, at denne navnedag havde været en af de behageligste, hun havde oplevet.

Nogle af de nærmeste slægtninge var endnu ikke taget hjem. De sad i den store salon. Fyrst Vasilij nærmede sig Pierre med trætte skridt. Pierre rejste sig og sagde, at det var sent. Fyrst Vasilij sendte ham et strengt, spørgende blik, som om det, Pierre netop havde sagt, var så mærkeligt, at man ikke kunne fatte det. Men så skiftede det strenge udtryk, og han trak Pierres hånd nedad, fik ham til at sætte sig ned og smilede kærligt.

»Nå, Ljolja?« sagde han, idet han straks vendte sig mod datteren med den ligeglade tone af indøvet ømhed, der er naturlig for forældre, der har forkælet deres børn fra vuggen, men som fyrst Vasilij kun havde tilegnet sig ved at efterligne andre forældre.
Og han vendte sig atter mod Pierre.
»Sergej Kuzmitj — Fra alle sider —« sagde han og knappede den øverste knap i sin vest op.

Pierre smilede, men hans smil viste, at han godt vidste, at det ikke var historien om Sergej Kuzmitj, der optog fyrst Vasilij lige nu, og fyrst Vasilij så, at Pierre vidste det. Han mumlede pludselig noget og gik ud. Pierre syntes, at selv fyrsten var bragt ud af fatning. Synet af den gamle verdensmands forlegenhed rørte Pierre: han kiggede på Hélène, og også hun syntes forlegen, og hendes blik syntes at sige: »Nå, det er din egen skyld.«

»Skridtet må tages, men jeg kan ikke, jeg kan ikke!« tænkte Pierre, og han begyndte atter at tale om ligegyldige ting, om Sergej Kuzmitj, og spurgte, hvad pointen med historien var, da han ikke havde hørt den ordentligt. Hélène svarede med et smil, at hun heller ikke havde fået den med.
Da fyrst Vasilij vendte tilbage til salonen, talte fyrstinden, hans hustru, med den ældre dame om Pierre med dæmpet stemme.
»Det er selvfølgelig et glimrende parti, men lykke, min kære...«
»Ægteskaber indgås i himlen,« svarede den ældre dame.
Fyrst Vasilij gik forbi, lod som om han ikke hørte damerne, og satte sig i en sofa i et fjernt hjørne af stuen. Han lukkede øjnene og syntes at døse. Hans hoved sank frem, og så rettede han sig igen.
»Aline,« sagde han til sin hustru, »gå hen og se, hvad de laver.«
Fyrstinden gik hen til døren, passerede den med en værdig og ligegyldig mine og tittede ind i den lille salon. Pierre og Hélène sad og talte som før.
»Stadig det samme,« sagde hun til sin mand.

Fyrst Vasilij rynkede brynene, hans mund fortrak sig, hans kinder sitrede, og hans ansigt antog det grove, ubehagelige udtryk, der var ham eget. Han rystede sig, rejste sig, kastede hovedet tilbage og gik med faste skridt forbi damerne ind i den lille salon. Med hurtige skridt gik han glad hen til Pierre. Hans ansigt var så usædvanligt triumferende, at Pierre rejste sig forskrækket ved synet.

»Gud ske tak!« sagde fyrst Vasilij. »Min hustru har fortalt mig alt!« (Han lagde den ene arm om Pierre og den anden om datteren.) »Min kære dreng... Ljolja... Jeg er meget glad.« (Hans stemme skælvede.) »Jeg elskede din far... og hun vil blive dig en god hustru... Gud velsigne jer!...«
Han omfavnede datteren og derefter atter Pierre og kyssede ham med sin ildelugtende mund. Tårerne fugtede virkelig hans kinder.
»Fyrstinde, kom herhen!« råbte han.

Den gamle fyrstinde kom ind og græd ligeledes. Den ældre dame brugte også sit lommetørklæde. Pierre blev kysset, og han kyssede den smukke Hélènes hånd adskillige gange. Efter en stund blev de atter ladt alene.

»Alt dette måtte ske og kunne ikke være anderledes,« tænkte Pierre, »så det er nyttesløst at spørge, om det er godt eller skidt. Det er godt, fordi det er afgjort, og man er fri for den gamle, pinende tvivl.« Pierre holdt sin forlovedes hånd i tavshed og betragtede hendes smukke barm, der hævede og sænkede sig.
»Hélène!« sagde han højt og holdt inde.
»Noget særligt siges altid ved sådanne lejligheder,« tænkte han, men kunne ikke huske, hvad det var, man sagde. Han så på hendes ansigt. Hun bøjede sig nærmere. Hendes ansigt rødmede.
»Åh, tag dem af... de dér...« sagde hun og pegede på hans briller.

Pierre tog dem af, og hans øjne — foruden det mærkelige udtryk, øjne har, når brillerne netop er taget af — havde også et forskræmt og spørgende blik. Han var ved at bøje sig ned over hendes hånd for at kysse den, men med en hurtig, næsten brutal bevægelse af hovedet opfangede hun hans læber og mødte dem med sine egne. Hendes ansigt slog Pierre ved sit forandrede, ubehageligt ophidsede udtryk.
»Det er for sent nu, det er afgjort; desuden elsker jeg hende,« tænkte Pierre.
»Je vous aime!« sagde han og mindedes, hvad man bør sige ved sådanne lejligheder: men hans ord lød så svage, at han skammede sig over dem.
»Jeg elsker Dem.«
Seks uger senere var han gift og bosat i grev Bezukhovs store, nymøblerede petersborgske hus, som lykkelig ejer — sagde folk — af en hustru, der var en berømt skønhed, og af millioner.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: In November 1805, Prince Vasili had to make an inspection tour of four different provinces. He had arranged this for himself so he could visit his neglected estates at the same time, pick up his son Anatole from his regiment, and take him to visit old Prince Bolkonsky to arrange a match with the rich old man's daughter. But before leaving home for these new tasks, Prince Vasili had to settle things with Pierre, who had lately been spending whole days at home—that is, at Prince Vasili's house where he was staying—and had been absurd, excited, and foolish in Hélène's presence (as a man in love should be), but had not yet proposed.

"This is all very well, but it needs to be settled," Prince Vasili said to himself with a sorrowful sigh one morning, feeling that Pierre—who was so deeply indebted to him (but never mind that)—was not handling this situation properly. "Youth, foolishness... well, God be with him," he thought, savoring his own generosity, "but it has to come to a head. The day after tomorrow is Lelya's name day. I'll invite two or three people, and if he still doesn't understand what he's supposed to do, then it becomes my responsibility—yes, my responsibility. I am her father."

Six weeks after Anna Pavlovna's party, and after the sleepless night when Pierre had decided that marrying Hélène would be a disaster and he should avoid her and leave, Pierre—despite that decision—had not left Prince Vasili's house. He felt with horror that in everyone's eyes he was being drawn closer to her every day, that he could no longer see her the way he used to, that he couldn't break away from her, and that although it would be terrible, he would have to tie his fate to hers. He might have been able to free himself, but Prince Vasili—who had rarely hosted gatherings before—now threw a party almost every evening at which Pierre had to be present unless he wanted to spoil everyone's enjoyment and disappoint their expectations. In the rare moments when he was home, Prince Vasili would take Pierre's hand in passing and draw it downward, or absent-mindedly offer his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek for Pierre to kiss, saying: 'See you tomorrow,' or 'Come to dinner or I won't see you,' or 'I'm staying in just for your sake.' And although Prince Vasili, when he stayed in 'for Pierre's sake,' barely exchanged two words with him, Pierre felt he couldn't let him down. Every day he told himself the same thing: 'It's time I figured out who she really is. Was I wrong before, or am I wrong now? No, she's not stupid, she's a wonderful woman,' he sometimes told himself. 'She never makes a mistake, never says anything foolish. She says little, but what she says is always clear and simple—so she can't be stupid. She was never embarrassed and isn't embarrassed now, so she can't be a bad person!' He had often started thinking aloud or making reflections in her company, and she always responded either with a brief, appropriate remark—showing it didn't interest her—or with a silent look and smile that more clearly than anything demonstrated her superiority. She was right to consider all arguments meaningless compared to that smile.

She always greeted him with a radiantly trusting smile meant just for him, a smile with something more significant in it than the general smile that usually brightened her face. Pierre knew that everyone was waiting for him to say a certain word and cross a certain line, and he knew that sooner or later he would cross it. But an incomprehensible terror seized him at the thought of that dreadful step. A thousand times during that month and a half, feeling himself drawn closer and closer to the terrible precipice, Pierre said to himself: 'What am I doing? I need willpower. Don't I have any?'

He wanted to make a decision, but realized with dismay that in this particular matter he lacked the strength of will that he knew he possessed and had demonstrated before. Pierre was one of those people who are strong only when they feel completely innocent, and ever since that day at Anna Pavlovna's when he was overcome with desire while leaning over the snuffbox, an unacknowledged sense of guilt about that desire had paralyzed his will.

On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me,' and so on.
"So he never got past 'Sergei Kuzmich'?" asked one of the ladies.

"Exactly—not one word further," answered Prince Vasili, laughing. "'Sergei Kuzmich... From all sides... From all sides... Sergei Kuzmich...' Poor Vyazminitov couldn't get any further! He would start the letter over and over, but every time he said 'Sergei' he would sob, then 'Kuz-mich'—tears—and 'From all sides' would be swallowed up in sobs, and he couldn't go on. And then the handkerchief again, and again: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides...' and more tears, until finally someone else had to read it."
"Kuzmich... From all sides... and then tears," someone repeated, laughing.
"Don't be cruel," cried Anna Pavlovna from her end of the table, wagging her finger. "He is such a fine, worthy man, our dear Vyazminitov..."

Everyone laughed heartily. At the head of the table, where the honored guests sat, everyone seemed to be in high spirits, excited by many things at once. Only Pierre and Hélène sat quietly, almost at the far end, with a suppressed smile on both their faces—a smile that had nothing to do with Sergei Kuzmich, a smile of self-consciousness about their own feelings. But however much the others laughed, talked, joked, and enjoyed their Rhine wine, sauce, and ices, however much they avoided looking at the young couple and seemed oblivious to them, everyone could sense from the occasional glances cast their way that the story about Sergei Kuzmich, the laughter, and the food were all a performance—that the true focus of everyone's attention was Pierre and Hélène. Prince Vasili mimicked Sergei Kuzmich's sobbing while glancing at his daughter, and even as he laughed, his expression clearly said: 'Yes... it's moving along, it will all be settled today.' Anna Pavlovna scolded him on behalf of 'our dear Vyazminitov,' but in her eyes, which briefly met Pierre's, Prince Vasili could read congratulations for his future son-in-law and his daughter's happiness. The old princess sighed sadly as she offered wine to the lady beside her and glanced angrily at her daughter, her sigh seeming to say: 'Yes, there's nothing left for you and me but to sip wine, my dear, now that these young ones are being so bold and shamelessly happy.' 'What nonsense I'm thinking!' thought a diplomat, looking at the lovers' happy faces. 'That's happiness!'

Into this trivial, artificial society had entered the simple power of attraction between a healthy, handsome young man and woman. And this human feeling rose above everything else, towering over all their affected chatter. Jokes fell flat, news failed to interest, and the liveliness was clearly forced. Not just the guests but even the servants waiting at table seemed to sense this, forgetting their duties as they gazed at the beautiful Hélène with her radiant face and at Pierre's broad, red, happy—though uneasy—face. It was as if the very candlelight focused only on those two happy faces.

Pierre felt that he was at the center of it all, which both pleased and embarrassed him. He was like a man completely absorbed in something. He couldn't see, hear, or understand anything clearly. Only now and then, disconnected ideas and impressions from the real world would flash unexpectedly through his mind.

"So it's all settled!" he thought. "But how did it happen? So quickly! Now I know it's not just because of her or just because of me, but because of everyone—it has to happen. They're all expecting it, they're so certain it will happen that I can't, I simply can't, disappoint them. But how will it turn out? I don't know—but it will definitely happen!" thought Pierre, glancing at those dazzling shoulders so close to his eyes.

Or he would suddenly feel ashamed without knowing why. He felt awkward attracting everyone's attention and being considered a lucky man—him, with his plain face, being seen as some kind of Paris who had won a Helen. 'But it always is this way and has to be!' he reassured himself. 'And besides, what did I do to bring it about? How did it start? I came from Moscow with Prince Vasili. Then nothing happened. So why shouldn't I stay at his house? Then I played cards with her and picked up her handbag and went driving with her. How did it start? When did all this happen?' And here he was sitting beside her as her fiancé, seeing, hearing, and feeling her nearness, her breathing, her movements, her beauty. Then it would suddenly seem that it wasn't she who was so beautiful, but he himself, and that's why everyone was looking at him. Flattered by this general admiration, he would puff out his chest, lift his head, and rejoice in his good fortune. Then suddenly a familiar voice repeated something to him for the second time. But Pierre was so lost in thought that he didn't understand.
"I'm asking when you last heard from Bolkonsky," Prince Vasili repeated a third time. "How distracted you are, my dear fellow."

Prince Vasili smiled, and Pierre noticed that everyone was smiling at him and Hélène. 'Well, so what if everyone knows?' thought Pierre. 'So what? It's the truth!' And he gave his gentle, childlike smile, and Hélène smiled too.
"When did the letter arrive? Was it from Olmütz?" repeated Prince Vasili, pretending he needed to settle a debate.
"How can anyone talk or think about such trivial things?" thought Pierre.
"Yes, from Olmütz," he answered with a sigh.

After supper, Pierre and his partner followed the others into the drawing room. The guests began leaving, some without saying goodbye to Hélène. Others came up to her briefly, as if unwilling to distract her from something important, and hurried away, not letting her see them out. The diplomat left the drawing room in mournful silence, reflecting on the pointlessness of his diplomatic career compared to Pierre's happiness. The old general grumbled at his wife when she asked about his leg. 'What an old fool,' he thought. 'That Princess Hélène will still be beautiful at fifty.'
"I believe congratulations are in order," Anna Pavlovna whispered to the old princess, kissing her warmly. "If I didn't have this headache, I would have stayed longer."
The old princess didn't reply. She was tormented by jealousy of her daughter's happiness.

While the guests were leaving, Pierre remained alone with Hélène for a long time in the small drawing room where they had been sitting. He had often been alone with her during the past six weeks but had never spoken of love. Now he felt it was inevitable, yet he couldn't bring himself to take the final step. He felt ashamed; he felt he was occupying someone else's place beside Hélène. 'This happiness is not for you,' some inner voice whispered. 'This happiness is for those who don't have what you have inside you.'
But since he had to say something, he asked if she had enjoyed the party. She replied in her usual simple way that it had been one of the most pleasant name days she could remember.

Some close relatives hadn't left yet and were sitting in the large drawing room. Prince Vasili approached Pierre with slow steps. Pierre stood up and said it was getting late. Prince Vasili gave him a look of stern puzzlement, as if what Pierre had said was too strange to process. But then the severity melted away, and he pulled Pierre's hand down, made him sit, and smiled warmly.

"Well, Lelya?" he said, turning instantly to his daughter with the casual tenderness that parents naturally show children they've spoiled since birth—though Prince Vasili had only learned this manner by imitating other parents.
And he turned back to Pierre.
"Sergei Kuzmich—From all sides—" he said, unbuttoning the top button of his waistcoat.

Pierre smiled, but his smile showed he knew it wasn't the story about Sergei Kuzmich that Prince Vasili was really interested in, and Prince Vasili saw that Pierre knew this. He suddenly mumbled something and walked away. It seemed to Pierre that even the prince was flustered. The sight of this worldly old man's discomfort moved Pierre. He looked at Hélène, and she too seemed flustered, her expression seeming to say: 'Well, it's your own fault.'

"The step has to be taken, but I can't, I can't!" thought Pierre, and he started talking about unimportant things again, about Sergei Kuzmich, asking what the point of the story was, since he hadn't heard it properly. Hélène smiled and said she had missed it too.
When Prince Vasili returned to the drawing room, his wife, the princess, was whispering to the elderly lady about Pierre.
"Of course it's a brilliant match, but happiness, my dear..."
"Marriages are made in heaven," the elderly lady replied.
Prince Vasili walked past, pretending not to hear them, and sat down on a sofa in a far corner. He closed his eyes as if dozing. His head drooped forward, then he roused himself.
"Aline," he said to his wife, "go see what they're doing."
The princess went to the door, walked past it with a dignified, indifferent air, and peeked into the small drawing room. Pierre and Hélène were still sitting and talking, just as before.
"Still the same," she told her husband.

Prince Vasili frowned, his mouth twisting, his cheeks twitching, and his face taking on the coarse, unpleasant expression that was characteristic of him. He shook himself, stood up, threw back his head, and strode purposefully past the ladies into the small drawing room. He walked up to Pierre with quick, joyful steps. His face was so unusually triumphant that Pierre rose in alarm.

"Thank God!" said Prince Vasili. "My wife has told me everything!" He put one arm around Pierre and the other around his daughter. "My dear boy... Lelya... I am so pleased." His voice trembled. "I loved your father... and she will make you a good wife... God bless you!"
He embraced his daughter, then Pierre again, and kissed him. Tears actually wet his cheeks.
"Princess, come here!" he called out.

The old princess came in and wept too. The elderly lady dabbed at her eyes with a handkerchief. Pierre was kissed, and he kissed the beautiful Hélène's hand several times. After a while they were left alone again.

"All this had to happen and couldn't have been otherwise," thought Pierre, "so there's no point asking whether it's good or bad. It's good because it's definite, and I'm free of the old tormenting doubt." Pierre held his fiancée's hand in silence, watching her beautiful chest rise and fall.
"Hélène!" he said aloud, and paused.
"You're supposed to say something special at a moment like this," he thought, but couldn't remember what people say. He looked at her face. She moved closer. Her face flushed.
"Oh, take those off... those..." she said, pointing at his glasses.

Pierre took them off, and his eyes—besides the strange look that eyes always have right after glasses are removed—also had a frightened, questioning expression. He was about to lean over and kiss her hand, but with a quick, almost rough movement, she intercepted his lips with her own. Her face, with its altered, unpleasantly excited expression, startled Pierre.
"It's too late now, it's done. Besides, I love her," thought Pierre.
"I love you!" he said, remembering what you're supposed to say at such moments. But his words sounded so feeble that he felt embarrassed.
"I love you."
Six weeks later he was married and settled in Count Bezukhov's large, newly furnished Petersburg house—the happy owner, as everyone said, of a beautiful, celebrated wife and millions of rubles.
